subject_entity.notes: Lost work by Marcion of Sinope, c. 140–144 AD. A systematic presentation of contradictions between the God of the Old Testament (just, wrathful) and the God revealed by Jesus (good, merciful). Foundational document of Marcionite theology. Known through refutations by Irenaeus (AH 1.27) and Tertullian (Against Marcion).

object_entity.notes: Wealthy shipowner from Sinope in Pontus; came to Rome c. 140; rejected the OT and constructed a reduced canon; excommunicated from the Roman church c. 144; major polemical target of Justin, Irenaeus, and Tertullian.

evidence.notes: Irenaeus describes Marcion composing his Antitheses to contrast the two gods.

passage.excerpt: Marcion of Pontus succeeded [Cerdo] and developed his doctrine, blaspheming with shameless effrontery Him proclaimed as God by the law and the prophets, declaring Him the author of evils, taking delight in war, infirm of purpose, and contrary to Himself. But Jesus, derived from that father above the God who made the world, came into Judaea in the times of Pontius Pilate, was manifested in the form of a man — abolishing the prophets and the law — but not truly taking flesh. He also mutilated the Gospel according to Luke, removing all that is written respecting the generation of the Lord.

object_entity.description: The Church accepts the Old Testament as authoritative Christian scripture; the God of creation and Israel is the same God as the Father of Jesus Christ. Denied by Marcion, Valentinus, Basilides, and most Gnostic schools.

evidence.notes: The entire Antitheses project contrasts the evil OT God with the good NT God — OT authority denied.

object_entity.proposition_label: Radical continence is required of all Christians
object_entity.description: Sexual continence, abstinence from meat, and/or abstinence from wine are required — not merely counseled — for all Christians; associated with Tatian, the Acts of Thomas, and some early Syriac communities.

evidence.notes: Eusebius HE 4.30 explicitly reports Tatian's encratite teaching and its spread.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Eusebius reports that Bardaisan of Edessa was at first a follower of Valentinus but later turned against the Valentinian heresy; he composed many dialogues in Syriac and Greek against the Marcionites and other heretics; despite his eloquent defense of the faith, he did not wholly purge himself of the old heresy.
